items.basis: The proposed bit-flip detection and correction mechanism fails to address the root cause of cache fragmentation in mixed-length bursty requests, which is spatial inefficiency rather than data corruption. The evidence [doi:10.1109/icassp55912.2026.11461518] shows that MIDAS framework focuses on dynamic cross-GPU cache offloading, not bit-flip issues, indicating this is a misdiagnosis of the problem.

The candidate fails to define boundary conditions for cache block sizes, bit-flip rates, or correction overhead. The evidence [doi:10.70675/036b4171z0acfz4a50z9d51z481b92e5f4da] on fundamental limits of shared-cache networks demonstrates that without precise boundary conditions, the solution will either overcorrect (wasting resources) or undercorrect (leaving vulnerabilities).

The candidate's own evidence [doi:10.5220/0015138800004103] on bit-flip vulnerability contradicts the intervention by showing that bit-flips are rare events (1 error per 10^18 bits) compared to cache eviction issues from fragmentation, making this solution a misallocation of engineering resources.

The intervention cannot beat the baseline because the predicted effect of reducing live-token evictions is not causally connected to bit-flip correction. The evidence [doi:10.14711/thesis-hdl152583] on resource-efficient model serving shows that eviction rates are primarily determined by cache allocation policies and request patterns, not data corruption.

Implementing bit-flip detection and correction in shared KV-cache blocks is impossible without significant performance degradation. The evidence [doi:10.5463/thesis.308] on latency-critical inference serving demonstrates that any added parity checks or correction algorithms would increase per-token processing time, directly counteracting the latency goals.

The testable prediction fails to pin down the specific bit-flip rate threshold that would trigger measurable improvements in eviction rates. Without this, the test cannot distinguish between the intervention's actual effects and normal system variance, as shown in the evidence [doi:10.5220/0015138800004103] which itself lacks clear metrics for when bit-flips become problematic.
